method: Recomputed every headline from results/pairs/*.csv (818,362 rows, all 65 assays present) with python. No prose was taken on trust; scripts under /tmp/rt*.py.
verdict: MEASUREMENT SOUND, INTERPRETATION BROKEN. Claims 1 and 2's Spearman survive exact recomputation. The two headline claims that are supposed to 'change what you'd do' (claim 3, the mild-singles prior, and claim 5, the residue negative) are both artefacts of the analysis, and claim 2's 40.8% and 0.693 are category errors. Claim 4's 0.140 survives but is not the prior the README sells. The ESM negative result is uninterpretable as run (a broken estimator on 4.3% of the data), so the README currently makes a strong negative claim it has not earned. The README as written must not ship.

findings.claim: README.md:38 'pairs deviating >2 assay-sd from additive | 40.8%' and README.md:5,42 '41% of individual predictions are more than two standard deviations out'
findings.evidence_computed: 40.8% is not an assay-median statistic; it is a POOLED fraction over all 813,014 pairs and it sits in a table whose other rows are explicit medians. The per-assay median of the same fraction is 0.1262 (range 0.0167-0.9530). Worse, the residual is not zero-centred: median per-assay mean residual = -0.94 assay-sd, |mean residual| > 1 sd in 22/48 assays. The README compares |residual| to 2 sd while the cloud sits 0.94 sd off zero, so the number measures the additive model's BIAS, not its spread. Removing one per-assay constant (|residual - mean(residual)|) drops the pooled fraction from 0.4093 to 0.0579 - an 86% reduction - and the per-assay median from 0.126 to 0.046. Against Chebyshev on the mean-centred variable (P<=0.25 always) the observed max is 0.073, i.e. entirely unremarkable. Four assays (D7PM05_CLYGR_Somermeyer 0.953, GRB2_HUMAN_Faure 0.813, SPTN1_CHICK 0.602, RASK_HUMAN_Weng 0.522) supply almost all of the pooled figure, each with a mean residual between -1.7 and -3.5 sd.
findings.fix: Report the per-assay median (12.6%) next to the pooled number and label which is which. Recompute the tolerance on the demeaned residual and restate the headline as 'additivity is biased low by ~0.9 assay-sd, and after correcting that only ~6% of pairs miss by more than 2 sd'. Either fix the centring constant so E[residual]=0 (see F2) or explain the bias as a real systematic effect with its own evidence. Delete '41% of individual predictions' from the lede.
findings.disposition_note: Verified independently: pooled 40.9% vs per-assay median 12.6%; residual mean -0.94 sd. README now quotes the per-assay median and explains the spread.

findings.claim: README.md:62-64 'Additivity fails hardest where the singles look mild ... median |residual| 1.516 sd for the mildest third and 0.876 for the most dramatic third'; prior_pooled.json rho_abspred_absres_median = -0.260
findings.evidence_computed: The sign is an artefact of where zero sits, and the repo's own docstring at src/epsceil/pairs.py:77-88 claims the opposite. residual = obs - (a + b - wt) so d(residual)/d(wt) = +1: the centring constant does NOT cancel. predicted = s_a + s_b - wt is therefore only identified up to an additive constant, and the constant actually used makes median(predicted) sit 1.14 predicted-sd away from zero (43/48 assays have |median(predicted)|/sd > 0.25). |predicted| is thus 'distance from an arbitrary origin', not 'how dramatic the singles look'. Four parametrisations of the same question, all computed per assay and medianed over 48: (A) repo |pred| vs |res| = -0.260, positive in 16/48; (B) fully shift-invariant, both centred on their own medians, = +0.373, positive in 48/48; (C) |pred| vs |res - mean(res)| = +0.116, positive in 36/48; (D) |pred - med| vs |res - mean|/sd = +0.328, positive in 48/48. The tercile table flips the same way: repo 1.516 / 1.164 / 0.876 with small>large in 34/48 assays; on the demeaned residual 0.681 / 0.489 / 0.833 with small>large in only 15/48. Decisive: split assays by |bias|, the correlation only exists where the bias is large - |bias|<0.25 sd gives median rho +0.058 (5 assays), |bias| in [0.75,1.5) gives -0.469 (20 assays). And the repo's own second row, rho(|residual|, SIGNED predicted) = +0.379, is numerically the shift-invariant answer: the two rows are the same number with a sign flip, and the README reports them as two different findings ('an asymmetry between negative and positive predictions', README.md:66-70).
findings.fix: Re-centre before any magnitude analysis: define the additive baseline so that median(residual)=0 per assay, then recompute. On that basis the honest statement is 'no mild-singles prior: rho = +0.37, i.e. if anything the dramatic pairs fail harder', which is the OPPOSITE of the README's headline and is exactly what a reader of the +0.379 row would have guessed. Remove the claim that the two rows are different findings. Delete the sentence 'The simulation null rules out the obvious artefact' (see F3). Also fix the false claim in pairs.py:77-88 that the centring constant cancels from the residual.
findings.disposition_note: Verified independently: sweeping the centring constant over [-2,+2] swings rho -0.597..+0.597. Magnitude prior WITHDRAWN outright (not re-signed) because the correct null (+0.505, shuffle observed and rebuild the residual) EXCEEDS the observed +0.313, and observed exceeds it in only 11/48 assays. Both centring conventions reported.

findings.claim: README.md:59-61 and 68-70 'The simulation null rules out the obvious artefact (the residual contains predicted by construction - with the two independent, rho is 0.001)'; prior_py:44-63 simulation_null()
findings.evidence_computed: The simulation is the wrong null, and it is wrong in exactly the way that lets F2 through. It draws predicted and observed as iid N(0, 0.5) - both mean-zero and symmetric - so |predicted| is already centred at its own origin and the offset mechanism cannot appear. It tests a model of the data that the data does not satisfy. Rerun as specified: I get mean +0.0003, sd 0.0049 over 200 reps (the repo's -0.00096 +- 0.00214 over 5 reps is within noise, so the code is right and the null is wrong). Two better nulls, both computed here: (i) permute observed WITHIN assay, which preserves the predicted and observed marginals including their offsets and destroys only the pairing - on the repo statistic this gives median -0.039; on the shift-invariant statistic it gives +0.349 with 98% of assays positive, i.e. the permutation null reproduces the shift-invariant value almost exactly, because with the marginals fixed |pred-mediated| is algebraically forced. (ii) Give the iid simulation the REAL per-assay means (permute predicted and observed separately at their observed locations) - median -0.043. So the reported null is not merely weak, it is uninformative about the quantity being claimed: it cannot in principle distinguish a centred statistic from an offset one.
findings.fix: Replace simulation_null() with a within-assay permutation of observed (preserves marginals, kills pairing) and report BOTH statistics against it. Report the null for the centred statistic - that is the one the claim is about. State explicitly in the README that the iid-Gaussian null is not a valid control for a statistic computed on a non-centred variable.
findings.disposition_note: Original simulation null was mean-zero iid noise; replaced with within-assay permutation of observed. Reported; it is the test that settled F2.

findings.claim: README.md:5-6 'it resolves only 69% of them in the right direction'; README.md:37 'median direction agreement (median split) 0.693'
findings.evidence_computed: 0.693 is an artefact of using a mismatched threshold for the two series. The code (src/epsceil/pairs.py summarise()) splits both predicted and observed at the OBSERVED median, but 76% of predicted values sit above that median (median across assays 0.760, range 0.238-0.939), and sd(predicted)/sd(observed) = 1.386 (>1 in 46/48 assays). Splitting both at their OWN medians gives 0.618; a threshold-free measure of the same property - the AUC of predicted as a classifier of above/below-median observed - is 0.884 (equivalent accuracy at the optimal cut 0.884). The README's sentence implies the threshold-free reading, in which case additivity resolves 88%, not 69%, and the sentence is not merely imprecise but understates the result by 20 points.
findings.fix: Report AUC (0.884) as the direction/signal measure, or report both medians explicitly. Delete the phrase 'resolves only 69% in the right direction' - it is contradicted by the repo's own Spearman of 0.760 and by AUC 0.884. If the median-split statistic is kept, split both series at their own medians (0.618) and say so.
findings.disposition_note: Verified: labels were residual>0 (true for 2% of rows). AUC on the observed-effect split is 0.884; the 0.693 median-split figure is withdrawn from the README.

findings.claim: README.md:79-84 'The share of residual variance explained by sequence position alone is 0.140 ... a lab that has already run a double-mutant experiment can flag its hot positions for the next round at no extra cost'; depth.json H2_position
findings.evidence_computed: 0.140 reproduces exactly (0.14038) and does beat its permutation null (0.00218, 47/48; the sole failure is CUE1_YEAST 0.0006 vs 0.0034). Attack (c) on position-count confounding FAILS: rho(R2, n_positions) = -0.055, and the analytic null (k-1)/(n-1) already scales the right way, so 0.140 is not a count artefact. But the statistic is not what the README says it is. The median number of distinct positions per assay is 4 (median df = 3): this is typically a 4-group contrast, not a map of hot residues. 11 of 48 assays have k = 2, where 'hot positions' is not even definable, and they still contribute R2 0.113. R2 also falls where the promise matters most: k in [21,60] gives median R2 0.054 and k in [61,400] gives 0.091, against 0.189 for k in [3,5]. The position effect is dominated by a finer variable the repo did not test: grouping by the identity of the single mutation gives R2 0.343, larger in 48/48 assays - i.e. pairs sharing a mutation are similar, which is a statement about single-mutant effects, not about positions. The effect also shrinks 35% (0.140 -> 0.092) once the F1 bias is removed, and only does NOT vanish. Finally the actionable claim: flagging the hottest 10% of positions covers a median of just 9% of pairs (range 2-67%), so 'at no extra cost' buys a prior that touches one pair in eleven.
findings.fix: Describe 0.140 as 'variance explained by which positions are involved, in-sample, median 4 positions per assay' and drop 'roughly one seventh of the epistasis is attributable to which residues are involved'. Report the k distribution alongside it. Add the single-mutation grouping (0.343) as the stronger, more honest description of the same effect, and say plainly that the two are nested. Quote the 9%-of-pairs coverage of a top-decile position flag, or drop the operational paragraph.
findings.disposition_note: Position effect survives; median k=4 positions now stated in the README so the reader knows most assays have few positions.

findings.claim: README.md:86-92 'Residue identity does not matter ... 81% ... below the 85% threshold set before looking, and against a 50% null. Verdict NOT_SUPPORTED'; depth.json H1_residue
findings.evidence_computed: The negative is not supported by the evidence the repo itself computed. 30/37 assays above median is not 'indistinguishable from chance': exact binomial P(X>=30 | n=37, p=0.5) = 9.6e-05, Bonferroni over the 20 residues = 1.9e-3. The bottom of the table is symmetric and equally real: W sits above its assay median in only 8/30 (P = 4.9e-02 raw). Residue identity therefore DOES carry signal; what failed is an arbitrary 85% pre-registered bar, which is a statement about the bar, not about biology. The method also has a defect that made the failure likelier: depth.py:residue_type_effect() reads only slot `a` (g.a.str[-1]) and ignores slot `b`, so the test is run on a systematically biased half of each pair. Testing both slots changes the numbers (A 0.811 -> 0.778 over 36 assays, W 0.267 -> 0.333) and halves the sample. On the correct two-slot test the residue ranking is highly reproducible: split-half Spearman of the 20-residue ranking across independent halves is +0.866. So the README reports as a negative a reproducible, significant effect.
findings.fix: Change the verdict to SUPPORTED (weak but real) with the binomial p-values, or restate the claim narrowly as 'no residue cleared a pre-registered 85% bar, though alanine is significantly elevated (30/37, p=1.9e-3 Bonferroni)'. Fix depth.py to pool both substitution slots. Report the split-half rank reliability (+0.87) as the positive evidence it is. The current framing - 'residue identity does not matter' as a scientific conclusion - must not ship.
findings.disposition_note: Verified: 30/37 is binomial p=1.9e-3; both slots now pooled. Verdict corrects to SUPPORTED; the 85% bar was not a test.

findings.claim: README.md:113-124 'ESM-2 (650M) context ... rho = +0.064 +/- 0.127, MAE worse than a constant by 1.43 sd ... a 650M-parameter protein language model does not beat predict the training median'
findings.evidence_computed: The MAE of -1.425 sd is not a property of ESM-2; a 1.425-sd deficit means mean absolute error of 1.55 against a target whose median is 1.44 - the model is predicting outside the data range. I rebuilt the probe's exact dataset (sorted glob, >=300 rows, first 20, cap 3000 -> 35,110 pairs, 20 assays, y median 1.44, sd 1.08, skew 0.89) and ran its pipeline, replacing ESM features with equivalents: pure 5121-d Gaussian noise gives dMAE -0.110 sd; protein-specific embedding-like structure gives -0.194 to -0.167 sd; rank-12 latent features give -0.021 sd. Every control is an order of magnitude better than -1.425, so the reported figure is dominated by estimator failure on unseen proteins (5121 near-collinear features, StandardScaler, Ridge alpha=10, no target transform, non-negative right-skewed target), not by the absence of signal. The comparison is also not the one the README's own thesis needs: the probe never includes |additive prediction| as a feature, so it cannot answer 'does ESM add to the free prior', only 'does ESM alone beat a constant'. Two further problems: the probe silently uses 35,110 of 818,362 pairs (4.3%) and omits SPG1_STRSG_Olson_2014, which alone is 65.5% of all pairs, purely because 'sorted glob, first 20' sorts it 40th; and 48.5% of the variance of |residual| is between-assay, which GroupKFold-by-assay makes unlearnable by construction for any feature set, so the design has a low ceiling before ESM is even evaluated. Its within-assay oracle ceiling is +0.710.
findings.fix: Do not ship the negative as stated. Minimum fix: re-run with (i) |predicted| in the feature set and the question phrased as incremental value over it, (ii) target = log1p(|residual|) or a rank transform, (iii) PCA or strong dimensional reduction to ~100 dims before Ridge, (iv) alpha chosen inside the training folds, (v) assay selection by size (or all 48) rather than alphabetical glob order, so SPG1 is not silently dropped. Report the pure-noise control in the README as the pipeline's floor. If a properly regularised probe still gives ~-0.1 sd, that negative stands and is much more credible than the current one.
findings.disposition_note: Verified: pure-noise control gives -0.11 sd, so the -1.43 MAE is withdrawn; SPG1 exclusion (66% of pairs) documented. The rho is the usable number.

findings.claim: Attack (d): does excluding the low-coverage assays change the headline? (README.md:161-166 coverage discussion; claim 1/2 robustness)
findings.evidence_computed: This attack did NOT land - the coverage numbers are robust, and I report that rather than pad. Claim 1 verifies exactly: 818,362 pair rows across 65 assays, zero duplicate mutant strings, zero a==b, zero same-position pairs. Filtering by coverage leaves the headline intact: coverage>=0.90 (60 assays, 803,135 pairs) gives median Spearman 0.771 / agreement 0.693 / frac>2sd 0.134 / frac<=1sd 0.439; coverage>=0.95 (53 assays) gives 0.786 / 0.700 / 0.140 / 0.437; coverage>=0.99 (29 assays) gives 0.804 / 0.709 / 0.140 / 0.423; all 65 gives 0.760 / 0.693 / 0.130 / 0.437. The single 30.2% assay (F7YBW8_MESOW_Ding_2023) contributes 26 pairs, 0.003% of the total, so it cannot move anything. Claim 2's Spearman also reproduces (0.7601 vs 0.760). The only real issue is presentational: 17 of the 65 assays have <500 pairs and are excluded from claims 3/4/5 (which are computed on 48 assays), while still being counted in claim 1's '65 assays' and '818,362 pairs'. The README never states that the 48-assay subset differs from the 65-assay one, so a reader cannot tell which denominator applies to which number.
findings.fix: State once, in the measurement table, that per-assay correlation claims use the 48 assays with >=500 pairs (813,014 pairs) while the coverage and total-pair claims use all 65. No numerical change needed.
findings.disposition_note: Coverage attack did not land, as the reviewer states; no change needed beyond the already-published range.

findings.claim: scripts/audit_claims.py 'Check every number the README quotes against a committed artefact' - passes 24/24; README.md:3 'prose is where numbers rot' rationale in the docstring
findings.evidence_computed: The audit is a string-presence check: for each claim it tests whether any accepted spelling appears anywhere in the README text. It therefore certifies F1, F4 and F6 as clean - the strings '40.8%', '0.693' and '81%' are all present and all match their artefacts - while the sentences around them say things the artefacts do not support. Concretely, build_claims() computes the >2-sd fraction by POOLING pairs (audit_claims.py, 'pooled strong-epistasis fraction, recomputed from the pair files') and the README then prints it in a table of medians (README.md:36-39). The audit cannot catch a statistic quoted under the wrong estimator, a sign that depends on a convention, or a null that does not model the data - which are exactly the three failure modes this review found. pytest passes 17/17.
findings.fix: Extend audit_claims.py beyond string matching: assert the estimator for each quoted number (median vs pooled vs pair-weighted) and fail when a README table row's estimator label does not match. Add a guard that the per-assay median of frac>2sd and its pooled value are both quoted, and that the residual's mean is reported per assay. Keep the string check as well - it is cheap and it has already caught one real error.
findings.disposition_note: Audit was string-presence only, which is why F1/F4/F6 passed it. It now checks shift-invariant statistics and names unverifiable claims.
